name: Karl Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. This is confidential. What happens in a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The courier drivers bring me fuel receipts before most of the office arrives. I'm Karl Jensen, forty-three, at Station Yard Accounting, and I prepare their accounts and tax returns. I earned a bachelor's in accounting after years dispatching vans, so I'm a junior on tax rules and still need my supervisor on unusual claims. I use the receipt assistant now and then after a colleague has tested it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Which part do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing why a toll appears on a route; the old dispatch map in my head helps. I hate finding a tax mistake after I've asked the supervisor to check the same thing twice. I cover the late courier appointments, which Station Yard pays above the usual rate because few people want those hours. My partner Ingrid teaches, our children are nine and thirteen, and we have a mortgage with eight months saved. There are plenty of similar firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could work with that. The receipt tool my colleague tried saves a few minutes on courier fuel claims, but it still calls a road toll a meal half the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should keep the modest shortcuts that pass a test. I'd tell the partners to leave a real person signing the return, because the courier doesn't care what produced a wrong tax bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be steady enough. I'm forty-three and junior at Station Yard Accounting because tax returns are newer to me than the dispatch work I used to do. The firm pays me more than most juniors for late courier appointments, Ingrid has a teaching wage, and we have eight months of expenses saved with plenty of firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paper fuel log beside the tested receipt tool and ask my supervisor to check the odd claims. I'd continue putting two hundred into savings each payday. In the first year of a plateau, I'd keep the late client slots and ask for one paid Friday review of my three recurring tax errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the mortgage and our two children. I'm slow on tax rules, but there is time to learn them without betting the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did your old job help catch an error?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One van driver wrote diesel on a toll receipt, and the tool believed the handwriting. I caught it because I used to price those routes. My tax knowledge still needs work, but my old dispatch memory is useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a paid review cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the supervisor the same three errors from last month and ask to review them during the quiet Friday hour. If the firm refuses paid time, I'd use its free training notes and keep asking for checks. I would not buy a course for a small change.

say: I would keep **tested shortcuts** on courier claims only after checking them against the paper fuel log.
I would insist a **person signs** every return.
think: Our **eight-month cushion** makes this future stable even if courier appointments slow.
My **tax rules** still need practice despite useful dispatch knowledge.
do: Keep the **fuel log** beside tested receipt sorting.
Deposit **two hundred each payday** into savings.
Review **three tax errors** if paid Friday time is granted; otherwise use free notes and keep supervisor checks.
feel: I feel **calm** about income and mortgage.
S0.quote: My tax knowledge still needs work, but my old dispatch memory is useful.
fieldNote: The **late-appointment premium** explains high pay without changing his junior tax standing.
His **dispatch memory** catches practical errors, while the eight-month reserve keeps a mild change calm.

steps.text: Keep paper fuel log and tested receipt sorter with supervisor checks
Deposit two hundred from each payday into household savings
Review three tax errors if paid Friday time granted
Use free notes and keep supervisor checks if paid review refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A stronger system could write the client reply, check the fuel entries and book the next appointment. Those are three jobs I do before lunch, so the late shift might get shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners to show hours saved beside errors and staffing plans. I'd tell colleagues we should test a system before trusting it, then pay people to learn the parts that remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose one late appointment shift a week, which is a meaningful slice of my higher pay. Ingrid's salary and our savings buy us time, but I don't want to spend the children's school fund on a work schedule that keeps shrinking. Plenty of firms are nearby, though they may use the same software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run a month-long comparison on twenty courier returns after another firm shows the tool is reliable. I'd take the wrong fuel and toll flags to our staff meeting and ask for paid time to learn the review screen. If my late shift is cut, I'd apply for a funded fleet-payroll post only if the advertised wage covers our mortgage and the written start time fits school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing part of my wage, with some choices still open. A small cut can be manageable if I see it coming and the other job is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a new shift do to school pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our youngest, Finn, gets collected at four on Thursdays. Ingrid teaches until five, so a new late shift needs a named person to do the pickup. We won't accept a job offer that leaves our youngest child waiting at school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the fleet offer show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fleet post would need a funded vacancy, the salary in writing and a confirmed start date. If any of those fail, I keep Station Yard's pay while I look. I'd rather argue over one late shift than jump to an unfunded promise.

say: I would seek **hours, errors and staffing** together.
I would ask for **paid review training** after a proper test.
think: My **late-shift premium** could fall as booking changes.
Nearby **firms** help, but their software may shrink jobs too.
do: Compare **twenty returns** after another firm proves the tool.
Take **wrong flags** to the staff meeting for paid training.
Seek **posted funded fleet work** after shift loss with written mortgage wage, confirmed start/pickup; otherwise retain Station Yard pay while searching.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing paid shifts.
S1.quote: We won't accept a job offer that leaves our youngest child waiting at school.
fieldNote: His **late-shift income** is exposed even though the household has a strong cushion.
The **fleet fallback** needs a funded post, written wage, confirmed start and reliable school pickup.

steps.text: Learn proven review tool by comparing twenty courier tax returns
Bring fuel and toll errors to staff meeting for paid training
Apply for funded fleet role after shift cut if written mortgage wage, start, pickup fit
Keep Station Yard pay while searching if fleet pay, start or pickup terms fail

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI by 2028 would do the figures and client letters faster than I can. The courier owner might still want a familiar face, but a familiar face may not justify our tax fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for notice and temporary wage support, then ask the partners for a plain headcount plan. I would not tell people the courier firms will keep buying a human return if the cheaper answer works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior tax job to end in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028. My work is thinking on a screen, so robots coming around 2031 do not add years to it. Ingrid's teaching wage and eight months saved give us a bridge, but nearby tax firms may all cut together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra mortgage payment and hold its three hundred a month in cash now. I'd apply for the funded depot dispatch vacancy if the posted wage covers our mortgage, the start date is written and the school pickup is covered. In the first year after 2028, if Station Yard ends my job, I'd claim wage support while using our reserve for regular bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing a good wage, even with eight months saved. I can picture the reserve dropping every month while I wait for a real vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could family cover the new job’s hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ingrid can cover ordinary school hours, not every late pickup. We'd ask her sister to help only if she agrees to the actual days, not as a line in my job application. I won't move the family timetable on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would dispatch stay safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatch post is also planning and screen work, so I would treat it as a bridge, not a safe career. I would ask the depot for a funded contract and a written wage before resigning. If it closes, I keep my current job until the partners make a decision.

say: I would seek **notice and wage support** if the tax firm cuts junior jobs.
I would ask for a plain **headcount plan**.
think: My **screen post** could end soon after 2028.
Eight months saved cannot guarantee a **new job** if firms cut together.
do: Hold **three hundred monthly** instead of extra mortgage payments.
Apply for **funded dispatch work** only with written mortgage pay, start and pickup; if closed, keep Station Yard pay.
Claim **wage support** after dismissal; ask Ingrid’s sister about pickup only if she agrees actual days.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing a good wage.
S2.quote: I won't move the family timetable on a guess.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches his tax desk in 2028; the later robot date offers no delay.
The **depot fallback** needs a funded contract, posted wage, written start and confirmed childcare.

steps.text: Hold three hundred monthly in cash instead of extra mortgage payments
Apply for funded dispatch post if written mortgage wage, start, pickup confirmed; otherwise keep job
Claim wage support after 2028 tax job loss
Ask partner’s sister for late pickup help only if she agrees to actual days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to test whether dispatch knowledge can earn a wage outside tax returns. I still expect the return itself to become cheap when full AGI arrives in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners to publish a plan and pay for learning while staff still have contracts. I'd ask for measured results rather than a promise that everybody will turn into an adviser.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might move into fleet compliance, visiting depots to check what the records say against actual vehicles. The reporting is thinking work and AGI may take much of it, so I would call it a possible bridge. Robots around 2034 do not protect the tax desk I have now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol in the fleet-compliance course if Station Yard funds the four-hundred fee and gives paid study hours. I'd inspect one depot vehicle file with a supervisor if the fleet operator grants a paid visit, then request written feedback. In the first year after AGI in 2031, if my tax post ends, I'd apply for a funded compliance vacancy only after that feedback and with posted mortgage-covering pay, a signed start and workable school-pickup hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years is enough to check the work in person. I do not want another certificate that only looks good in a folder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask your firm to pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course fee would fit our savings, but I want the practice to pay if it wants to sell fleet checks. If it refuses the fee or paid hours, I would keep my Station Yard wage and use free transport-safety talks instead. That is learning, though it is not a placement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful depot visit include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A supervisor should let me compare a vehicle's actual maintenance card with the submitted expense record. If the visit is only a tour, I won't claim I can audit a fleet. I'd ask for written feedback before I apply for the vacancy.

say: I would seek **funded learning** with a real work plan.
I would ask for **measured results** before promises.
think: A **fleet compliance** role may use my old dispatch experience outside routine tax returns.
AGI could also take its **screen reporting**.
do: Enrol in **fleet study** if fee and hours are funded; otherwise keep Station Yard pay and use free talks.
Inspect a **real vehicle file** on paid supervision and get written feedback before applying.
Apply after **2031 tax job loss** only for funded compliance work with posted mortgage pay, signed start and pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but able to test the role.
S3.quote: I do not want another certificate that only looks good in a folder.
fieldNote: **Firm-funded study** and a real depot file test his possible move beyond tax returns.
The **compliance application** requires post-2031 job loss, a funded vacancy, posted pay and workable pickup hours.

steps.text: Enrol in fleet course if firm pays fee and hours; otherwise use free talks
Inspect real vehicle file on paid supervised visit if fleet grants access
Get written supervisor feedback before applying for fleet compliance vacancy
Apply after 2031 tax job loss for funded post with mortgage wage, start, pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets me be careful. Finn would be almost grown by 2036, and our other child would already be making choices about work or study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for shorter working weeks as returns get quicker and for training tied to actual openings. I would also want a public backstop if an employer takes the savings and leaves staff to pay for their own move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect routine accounts and returns to shrink when thinking AI reaches full strength in 2036. Visiting depots might give me work built on trust and records, but a funded employer has to want it. Robots around 2039 do not lengthen my accounting desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the courier appointments for now and ask the transport association next spring about a funded field-audit traineeship. I would join only with paid supervised visits, a posted wage above our mortgage need and a confirmed start that fits our remaining school pickup. In the first year after 2036, if the tax desk closes, I'd take a funded field-audit vacancy only with written mortgage-covering pay, signed start and workable pickup; otherwise I'd claim support and keep searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with years to gather proof. We can afford to wait for a real opening instead of chasing a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What place do the children have in this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not want either child planning to pay our mortgage. The older one may be working by then, but that money is for their life. We'd keep the household reserve in our own names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the traineeship has no paid place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the association which employer funds the traineeship and who supervises the visits. If it cannot name a paid place, I keep the Station Yard wage and attend free depot open days. I would not resign for an invitation to observe.

say: I would seek **shorter weeks** and real training openings.
I would support a **public backstop** for unfunded moves.
think: My **tax desk** still shrinks by 2036 even with ten years to prepare.
A **field-audit job** needs a funded employer.
do: Keep **courier appointments** and attend free depot days if no paid place opens.
Join a **funded traineeship** only with paid visits, wage, start and pickup.
After **2036 tax job loss**, take a funded audit vacancy with written mortgage pay, start and pickup; otherwise claim support and search.
feel: I feel **uneasy** while waiting for proof.
S4.quote: I would not resign for an invitation to observe.
fieldNote: The **ten-year horizon** supports slow testing while preserving current high pay.
The **field-audit path** requires funded supervision, a mortgage-covering wage, confirmed start and workable childcare.

steps.text: Keep courier appointments and attend free depot days if no funded traineeship
Join funded field-audit traineeship only with paid visits, mortgage wage, start and pickup
Take funded audit vacancy after 2036 tax loss if written mortgage wage, start, pickup confirmed
Claim support and keep searching after 2036 tax loss if no funded audit vacancy

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could end my desk job before a depot has a funded place. Notice, temporary wages and paid field training tied to a real vacancy would help. Eight months of savings buys choices, but not a permanent wage. Our children still need a pickup plan, not just an offer letter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how employers prove a new job exists. I would want the posted wage, the start date and the person supervising me. A course brochure is easy to print; a payroll place is harder to promise.

headlineQuote: A course brochure is easy to print; a payroll place is harder to promise.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Karl is a junior tax accountant serving couriers after years dispatching vans.
His **accounting bachelor’s** and late client hours bring high pay despite tax skills he is still learning.
He uses **AI occasionally** after colleagues test it and keeps a paper fuel log.
A **mortgage**, two schoolchildren and eight months saved give choices, with plenty of nearby firms.
He tests **fleet work** only with funded training, posted pay and reliable pickup hours.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his screen job before a depot offers funded work.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **notice**, temporary wages and paid field training linked to a real vacancy.
